Battle of the Little Bighorn. A devastating defeat inflicted on the United States seventh Cavalry regiment by combined Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors led by Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse in June eighteen seventy-six. The battle represented the Indian tribes' last major collective victory against American expansion. Yet it also provoked a crushing federal response that shattered Native American resistance and led to the final conquest and reservation confinement of the Great Plains tribes.

The battle occurred on June twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth, eighteen seventy-six, in the Little Bighorn River valley in Montana during the Great Sioux Wars. Sitting Bull, a Lakota holy man and strategist, organized a massive encampment of thousands of warriors from multiple tribes resisting forced reservation relocation.

George Armstrong Custer, pursuing glory and Native American scalps, attacked without waiting for reinforcements or respecting Native American strength. His regiment was outnumbered and overwhelmed. All two hundred sixty-eight soldiers and scouts under his direct command were killed, including Custer himself.

The shocking defeat galvanized American public opinion and military response. The federal government launched overwhelming campaigns that within months forced surviving tribes onto reservations. The battle became known as Custer's Last Stand, a symbol of Native American resistance and a turning point in the Indian Wars. After this battle, tribal autonomy effectively ended on the Great Plains.

It connects to Sitting Bull the Lakota spiritual and military leader who orchestrated the tribal alliance and battle strategy, to the Cheyenne who were one of the primary warrior peoples, and to the broader Indian Wars between the United States and Native American peoples for control of the continent.
